claims.text: Tempered martensitic steel intentionally alloyed with small amounts of embrittling impurities can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition as a function of testing temperature.
Phosphorus can act as an embrittling impurity in tempered martensitic steel.
Controlled impurity additions followed by suitable heat treatments promote grain-boundary segregation at intermediate temperatures.
The relevant structural mediator is temperature-dependent segregation of impurity atoms such as phosphorus to grain boundaries.
At low temperatures, the impurity atoms remain relatively immobile.
Tempered martensitic steel containing the introduced impurities remains ductile at low testing temperatures.
Entering an intermediate temper-embrittlement window enhances impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
Impurity segregation weakens grain boundaries and causes brittle behavior in the intermediate temperature range.
Further heating homogenizes the impurity distribution or dissolves grain-boundary segregation.
Removal or homogenization of grain-boundary segregation restores ductility at higher temperatures.
The predicted response is ductile behavior at low temperature, brittle behavior in a narrow intermediate range, and renewed ductile behavior at higher temperature.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys suppress temper embrittlement.
High configurational entropy and reduced impurity segregation are responsible for suppression of temper embrittlement in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys.
The proposed transition requires controlled impurity levels and specific heat treatments.
The transition temperature window and critical impurity concentration vary with alloy composition and processing.
